title: Family worship
hookLine: Reformed and Puritan homes read and prayed together daily

lines: NOT JUST SATURDAY NIGHT. EVERY DAY.
cards: A poem by Robert Burns follows a Scottish farm laborer home at the end of the week. Supper is over. The family pulls in around the fire.
The father takes down the big family Bible, the one that was his own father's pride, and lays his cap aside. They sing a psalm. Then, Burns writes, "The priest-like father reads the sacred page."
And he prays. A poet's picture, and a tender one. But in Reformed and Puritan homes, a scene like that wasn't meant for one Saturday night.
It was meant for every day.

teach.h: WHEN THOU SITTEST IN THINE HOUSE.
teach.b: Reformed Christians found the idea in the Bible.

teach.h: AS FOR ME AND MY HOUSE.
teach.b: Moses tells Israel to keep God's words on their hearts, and "teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."
Home, road, bed, morning: faith spoken at the kitchen table, not only at the altar. Joshua says it in one line: "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."

teach.h: THE CHURCH THAT IS IN THEIR HOUSE.
teach.b: And Paul greets Priscilla and Aquila and "the church that is in their house." A household could be a small church.
The Church of Scotland set out a directory for worship at home: households were to pray together, read the scriptures, and sing praises, with the head of the house leading.

teach.h: A PSALM, A CHAPTER, A PRAYER.
teach.b: The shape was simple: a psalm sung, a chapter read, a question or two for the children, a prayer. It doesn't wait for Sunday, or for the minister.
The father or mother who was arguing over the bills an hour ago now opens the book. The children who fidgeted through supper hear the same stories their grandparents heard.
And for a few minutes the kitchen becomes a place of worship.
Not every home looked like Burns's poem, and homes now look all kinds of ways: a single parent and a teenager, roommates, a couple, a grandmother and one grandchild.
Some Christians keep the old pattern with a devotional book at breakfast. Some pray together at bedtime. The furniture changes.
The idea stays: a household that stops, together, and turns toward God.

how: In some Reformed, Presbyterian and other Protestant homes, families keep daily family worship: reading a passage of scripture, singing a psalm or hymn, and praying together, often after a meal or before bed.

practice: If someone is nearby, ask whether you can read them something short, like Psalm one twenty-one: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help."
If you're alone, read it aloud anyway, keeping in mind the people you share a roof or a table with, or once did. Then sit quietly a moment, and if you pray, name each of them before God.
